activities.anchor: Every soundtrack is a blend of four strata
activities.caption: pair each stratum with its job
activities.name: sdLayerMatch

config.prompt: Four strata, four jobs — pair each layer with the work it does:

pairs.right: the spine — audiences forgive almost anything except unintelligible words
the world's body: doors have weight, punches thud, weapons sing
the room's breath — a cut with dead air sounds like the world stopped
lines re-recorded in a studio to patch failed location sound — at the cost of a sheen

config.why: The mix balances all four across the film's arc, in formats from stereo to 5.1/7.1 surround to Dolby Atmos's object-based system — sounds placed in 3-D space rather than assigned to channels.

config.text: Ben Burtt built Star Wars's audio world from synthesis and junk: the lightsaber's hum is a broken %%0%%'s interference blended with an old film %%1%%'s motor, and R2-D2 speaks in an %%2%% synthesiser layered with the designer's own whistles.
config.hint: A television, a projector, and an ARP — audiences heard 'reality'; they were hearing design.

activities.anchor: good recordist just captures them well
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the recordist's brief
activities.name: sdRealSpot

config.prompt: One line of this recording brief is wrong — click it:
lines: On-set microphones chase dialogue and miss the intimate texture layer.
Footsteps, cloth and props are performed to picture in a studio.
Ambience is layered from libraries; hard effects are designed.
The real sound of a thing is usually the right one for the story.
The craft records a lie that carries the moment's truth better than reality would.
config.correction: The real sound is usually wrong for the story — too thin, too quiet, too literal.
config.why: Coconut halves clop for horses, frozen celery snaps for broken bones, a heavy telephone book thumps under every movie punch you have ever believed — the sound is a lie, the belief is real.

activities.anchor: grammar parallel to the shot ladder
activities.caption: drag the divider — the mix breathes with the cut
activities.name: sdPerspectiveCompare

config.prompt: The same sequence, two cut sizes — drag the divider and listen:

before.label: Picture cuts wide
before.text: The world's acoustics re-enter: room tone, wind and traffic refill the track — the space stays big and social.

after.label: Picture cuts closer
after.text: The soundtrack dries out and personalises: ambience recedes, breaths arrive — the frame tightens around one interior.

config.why: Off-screen sound extends the frame further still: a creak behind the protagonist tells you the room is bigger than the image — the monster you hear is scarier than the one you see.

activities.caption: file each cue: with, against, or silent
activities.name: sdScoreBuckets

config.prompt: Three strategic choices — file each scoring move:

items.label: Herrmann's strings are the knife in Psycho's shower (1960)
Williams's two-note shark theme returning with its history
"Singin' in the Rain" over a home invasion
needle-drops over napalm in Apocalypse Now
the dread stretch of No Country for Old Men runs on ambience alone
A Quiet Place makes quiet the premise

config.why: Aligned scoring tells the audience how to feel; counterpoint delivers irony the characters cannot access; silence removes the floor — and spending the whole dynamic range from minute one exhausts the instrument the drama needs.

activities.caption: line up the hand-offs, location to delivery
activities.name: sdPipelineOrder

config.prompt: The soundtrack's relay — line up the hand-offs in order:
items: Production sound — the location mixer captures clean dialogue
Sound editorial — repair, ADR, library and original effects
Foley — the intimate layer performed to picture
Music — the score arrives from the composer's side
Re-recording mixers — thousands of tracks blended into 7.1 / Atmos
config.why: Every stage trades against the others: an M&E (music-and-effects) version is built under the dialogue for foreign-language dubbing, and the intelligibility problem is usually a chain decision, not one mixer's whim.

activities.anchor: Sound design's conventions bend by form
activities.caption: three briefs, three contracts with the listener
activities.name: sdFormBranch

config.root: Three briefs land on your desk this week. Each one carries a different contract with the listener.

start.text: Brief one: a documentary. What does its soundtrack honour?

choices.label: The honesty contract — ambience and interview carry it; music supports, never argues
choices.feedback: Over-scoring a documentary reads as manipulation — and the field recordist's wind protection and room tone are the genre's invisible foundation.

choices.label: Total design — invent every sound from nothing
choices.feedback: That is animation's contract, not documentary's: here the world exists and must be recorded honestly.

anim.text: Brief two: an animated short. Why are animation stages the craft's laboratory?

choices.label: Nothing real exists to record — every sound is invented, and cartoon physics trains designers
choices.feedback: The slide-whistle fall and the sprung spring trained generations whose live-action work hides the artifice better.

choices.label: Libraries supply everything, as in live action
choices.feedback: There is no location to record from — no library holds a world that was never real.

game.text: Brief three: a game. What happens to the timeline?

choices.label: It dissolves — sounds become systems triggered by play: footsteps vary by surface, adaptive music shifts with danger
choices.feedback: The designer becomes a programmer of behaviour rather than an arranger of events.

choices.label: It stays fixed, as in a film
choices.feedback: Game audio abandons the timeline: barks and stingers are queued by state machines, not arranged on a track.

end.text: Three forms, three contracts — and one transferable lesson underneath.

config.why: Audiences accept any acoustic world, real or invented, provided its internal logic never breaks.

activities.anchor: The auditory system's design explains the craft
activities.caption: true or false — the ear's head start
activities.name: sdPsychoJudge

statements.s: The ear processes onsets faster than the eye resolves detail.
statements.why: Sound arrives with a head start — which is why the soundtrack decides whether a space feels vast or airless before the eye has voted.

statements.s: The ventriloquist effect is the brain binding a sound to whatever visual source plausibly produced it.
statements.why: It is why a lip-synced frame reads as a speaking mouth — and why Foley works at all.

statements.s: Accepting off-screen sound requires a deliberate suspension of disbelief.
statements.why: The ear accepts sources the eye never sees — no suspension required, which is precisely why off-screen sound is so cinematic.

statements.s: Sound localises on the scale of whole seconds.
statements.why: Milliseconds — sound localises fast and triggers the orienting head-turn reflex.
